opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. When I joined, the team was small enough that everyone basically knew what everyone else was working on. You could just turn around and ask someone. That doesn't scale. As you grow, the default is that communication overhead eats into the time people spend actually doing the work.

A few things seem to matter most to me.

**Clear ownership.** On a small team you can get away with fuzzy boundaries because people sort things out informally. On a bigger team, if it's unclear who owns a decision, either nobody makes it or three people make it differently. So we try to be explicit about who's responsible for what, especially on something like pretraining where many pieces have to fit together.

**Hiring for people who are self-directed.** The best people I've worked with don't need much management. They see a problem, figure out whether it matters, and go fix it. If you hire people who need constant direction, adding headcount can make you slower, because you're adding coordination cost without adding much independent progress.

**Protecting focus time.** It's easy for engineers and researchers to end up in meetings all day as the org grows. I try to be skeptical of new recurring meetings and push toward written updates people can read asynchronously.

**Accepting that some things will get worse.** You won't keep the exact feel of a ten-person team when you're much bigger. The goal is to make sure the work that matters most still moves quickly, even if some things get a bit more bureaucratic.

There's also a mission angle. People here care a lot about why we're doing this. That shared sense of purpose does a lot of coordination work for free. If everyone is pointed at the same goal, you don't have to align them as explicitly. I think that's one of the most underrated things for staying productive while growing.

r001.rationale: The response does not say productivity should increase in proportion to headcount; it focuses on keeping important work moving quickly despite growth.

r002.rationale: It says that as the team grows, communication overhead eats into time spent doing the work, making it harder for productivity to keep pace.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a really hard problem, and honestly it's one I think about a lot. When I joined, the pretraining team was tiny — you could fit everyone in a room, and coordination was basically just talking to the people next to you. Everyone knew what everyone else was doing. As you grow, that stops working, and you have to be much more deliberate about it.

The way I think about it is that there's this tension between adding more people and keeping the per-person productivity high. The naive model is that if you double the team, you get double the output. That's basically never true. There's communication overhead, there's onboarding cost, there are more people who could step on each other's toes when they're all touching the same codebase or the same training runs. So the question is how much of that doubling you actually capture.

A few things I think matter a lot. One is that you want to hire people who can work fairly independently and who have good judgment, because the more you have to specify every task in detail, the more the bottleneck becomes the people doing the specifying. You want to give people a clear sense of the goal — what are we actually trying to achieve — and then let them figure out the path.

Another is investing in the infrastructure and tooling early. When you're small, you can get away with a lot of hacky stuff because the people who wrote it are the ones using it. Once you've got a bunch of new people who weren't there when the hacks were made, that stuff becomes a huge tax. So spending time on making things robust and well-documented pays off, even though it feels slow in the moment.

And then there's just the culture piece. I think it's important that people feel empowered to point out when something's broken or when a process doesn't make sense, rather than just routing around it. A lot of inefficiency at scale comes from people quietly working around problems that could have been fixed if someone had raised them.

I'll also say that I don't think we've fully solved this. It's an ongoing thing. Every time the team grows significantly, some set of processes that used to work stops working, and you have to notice that and adjust. The trick is noticing it quickly rather than six months later.

r001.rationale: It describes keeping per-person productivity high as the team grows and contrasts that with the goal of doubling output when the team doubles.

r002.rationale: It identifies communication overhead as a reason doubling the team does not produce double the output.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is that adding people doesn’t automatically translate into getting more done. You also add communication overhead, and you can end up in a situation where everyone is working hard but spending more of their time coordinating with one another.

So I’d think about it in terms of how you give teams clear ownership and enough context to make decisions independently. If every decision has to go through a small number of people, those people become bottlenecks as the organisation grows. But if you split everything up without maintaining a shared understanding of what matters, teams can end up pulling in different directions.

There’s also a short-term versus long-term tradeoff. Bringing someone on takes time from people who are already productive. You have to be willing to make that investment, while being thoughtful about how much change a team can absorb at once. The thing I’d want to keep asking is: are we actually getting better at doing the most important work, or are we just getting bigger?

r001.rationale: It says adding people does not automatically mean getting more done, but does not identify productivity increasing in proportion to headcount as the ideal outcome.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies added communication overhead and coordination time as reasons productivity may not keep pace as the team grows.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is that adding people doesn’t automatically mean you get proportionally more done. You also create more communication overhead, and it becomes harder for everyone to understand what matters most and who’s responsible for what.

So you need to get better at giving teams clear goals and enough context to make decisions independently. If every decision has to go through the same small set of people, those people become a bottleneck. But if you just delegate without sharing the reasoning behind the priorities, teams can end up pulling in different directions.

There’s also a balance between building processes that help at your current size and preserving the ability to move quickly. I’d want us to keep asking: is this actually helping people do useful work, or is it just creating more work around the work?

r001.rationale: Saying that adding people does not automatically yield proportionally more work done treats proportional productivity growth as the expected benchmark.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says added communication overhead makes it harder to maintain productivity as the team grows.
